pr_body:
Modified rand_cpu_x86.c to support builtin hardware randomizer on HPE NonStop.

CLA: Permission is granted by the author to the OpenSSL team to use these modifications.
Fixes #12903

Signed-off-by: Randall S. Becker <rsbecker@nexbridge.com>

> 
> 
> Why would an x86 processor support RDRAND but not support the CPU flags indicating it's usability? This seems pretty odd to me.

I think I have an (speculative) answer on this. Looking purely at the timing of events, the c99 compiler was developed by one group many years ago. The externalization of the RDRAND ops were added by request to a different group much more recently and likely did not include requested changes to the compiler(s), or approval was not given for that. This may be resolved when we get a more recent compiler made available but I have no timeframe on when that will be - very much outside my control.

@paulidale Once PR #12933 is merged, I'll have a fixup for this PR to update the define used for selecting TANDEM. I think that's the last change needed.

>Any entropy that is present will be in the low order bits of the TS_NANOSECS_(). So maybe TS_NANOSECS_() & 15. The exact number of bits is difficult to estimate: it requires data collection and a lengthy statistical analysis and even then it could be wrong.

Previous experience with this has shown that even some of the lower bits need to get masked out because of repeated patterns in the bits.. As Pauli says - Validating and justifying an entropy source can be very time consuming.

I think you're at least misunderstanding the question. All x86
since the pentium in 1993, and all x86_64 CPUs support the CPUID
instruction. That instruction allows us to find out that RDRAND is
available or not. We have assembler support in
crypto/x86_64cpuid.pl that should allow is to detect if RDRAND is
available or not. The compiler is not involved.

It can be that the OS is masking certain CPU features, and that
even when the CPU supports it, we can't see it.

The compiler is not involved. It can be that the OS is masking certain CPU features, and that even when the CPU supports it, we can't see it.

I understand, but the instructions are not being detected. Perhaps it is because there is no assembler on this platform and the ELF formats are slightly different. There are also two variants, one is x86 (big endian), the other is ia64 (big endian). I've been through the lack of detection of features in many products, and may be the OS, so this is not a surprise. I can't control that part of things.

Is there a reason you don't use the assembler? Is it using a
different ABI? Not using the assembler will mean that you don't
use various CPU support like AESNI which will make it slower.

I'm pretty sure x86 only supports little endian, while ia64 can
switch between big and little endian. Maybe what you mean is that
like VOS, all data is stored in big endian, and you have the
compiler convert it on load and store?

> 
> Is there a reason you don't use the assembler? Is it using a different ABI? Not using the assembler will mean that you don't use various CPU support like AESNI which will make it slower. I'm pretty sure x86 only supports little endian, while ia64 can switch between big and little endian. Maybe what you mean is that like VOS, all data is stored in big endian, and you have the compiler convert it on load and store?

1. There is no available assembler on the platforms (TNS/E-itanium, or TNS/X-x86), not for a lack of trying to get one for years. gcc is also not available either or we would be using it. While objects are ELF format, they are not standard.
1. The x86 big-endian is implemented in custom millicode on the TNS/X platform.

From what I read online, it's the compiler (and OS) that converts it to big endian.

The 2 timestamps might have a different starting point and resolutions, but they are most likely generated from the same hardware clock.

> 
> 
> From what I read online, it's the compiler (and OS) that converts it to big endian.
> 
> The 2 timestamps might have a different starting point and resolutions, but they are most likely generated from the same hardware clock.

They are not generated by the same hardware clock. CPU coldload times are real-time clocks in each CPU and are independent. The System clock is an aggregate of the DateTime Clock from all CPUs and synchronises/self-corrects/publishes via the message system. They two are actually very unrelated. The DateTime clock is subject to a large amount of actual drift and it takes regular updates from NIST to keep it sane.
Rechecking uint64_t. Not posting anything relating to Itanium in this pull request. That will be a separate one if we go there.

I'm not sure I understand why this PR has issues.  Sure, @openssl/committers are often used to Linux or similar and the offer of a multitude of free compilers / assemblers, and here comes code for a platform very few of us have a good idea of, apart from manuals we can find on the net.  For this section of code, I don't think we have any other option than to trust @rsbecker's knowledge...  and it shouldn't matter for the rest of us, as it's guarded well enough.

And sure, some *future* fixes may do a better job of checking CPUID and find out all sorts of stuff, and starting to use the assembler code we have.  It doesn't have to happen now.  If this code is the difference between "working" and "not working" for NonStop machinery, that should be good enough for now.
(it took a looooong time before VMS builds started using the assembler code, at all, FYI...)

> The `TS_NANOSECS_()` method returns nanoseconds since the last system cold-load while `JULIANTIMESTAMP()` returns microseconds since about the creation of the world in biblical tradition. The two are independent. 

No they are **not** independent.  The two are _extremely_ correlated: each advances one second per second.  In terms of randomness obtainable, a second timer adds effectively nothing.


I don't believe that [Julian Day Numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day#Julian_Period) are biblical in origin...

> 
> 
> > The `TS_NANOSECS_()` method returns nanoseconds since the last system cold-load while `JULIANTIMESTAMP()` returns microseconds since about the creation of the world in biblical tradition. The two are independent.
>

> 
> I don't believe that [Julian Day Numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day#Julian_Period) are biblical in origin...

Just for info: on this platform, `JULIANTIMESTAMP() == 0` corresponds to 12:00 UTC on January 1, 4713 B.C. The number is computed software clock aggregated across processors. Each of the 16 logical CPUs has their own real time clock that the 6 IPUs use for the `TS_NANOSECS()`. There is rarely any correlation even at 10 parts per 10000 between the two clocks with the former being in software and the latter being in hardware.

Before anything is done for the Itanium box, in a separate PR/Issue, I will be subjecting any random generator that uses these to a heavy weight battery test to assess randomness. This is not happening here. I will communicate the results of the tests. If I cannot get even the NIST tests to pass (a subset of what I am testing), that PR won't see the light of day. Ever. Aside from that, the box (TNS/E) goes off support in 2.5 years, so this may be a moot point if I can't get this to work by then. ;)

I find the NIST tool very useful: https://github.com/usnistgov/SP800-90B_EntropyAssessment

> I find the NIST tool very useful: https://github.com/usnistgov/SP800-90B_EntropyAssessment

There are some serious problems with the NIST tooling.  The restart tests e.g. fail a significant percentage of the time even with truly random data.  I can't find the reference to the rebuttal of the tests -- it was presented at ICMC two years back.

> There is rarely any correlation even at 10 parts per 10000 between the two clocks with the former being in software and the latter being in hardware.

Without disputing how the two clocks actually work, I would still assume that they both (mostly) increment...  I don't have the deep knowledge of randomness that others have, and still, just that assumption makes red flags go wild in my head.
Generally speaking, using clocks as a source of entropy is considered a bad choice.  I suspect people would otherwise abuse NTP for that sort of thing.
It's the only tool I know that's designed to test the raw input. All others I know look at the output of the RNG.
You probably mean: https://www.untruth.org/~josh/sp80090b/Care%20and%20Feeding%20of%20SP800-90B%20D12.pdf
Yes, it was Josh Hill who discovered the worst of it.  I submitted a few comments which were mostly addressed in the final revision.  The committee has been refining things since then.
There is also this very recent presentation: https://www.untruth.org/~josh/sp80090b/90B%20Extravaganza%2020200921.pdf, and  new repository: https://github.com/KeyPair-Consulting/Theseus

issue_context.title: Add hardware randomizer capability on NonStop x86 architecture
issue_context.body:
The default implementation of randomization functions do not include the hardware randomizer available on HPE NonStop x86. This is needed because the operating system does not support `/dev/random` or `/dev/urandom` and EGD is not allowed by FIPS.

This applies to version 3.0.0. I am volunteering to implement this capability.

Note: This capability is not available for the NonStop Itanium port.
comments:
There are two possible calls available to do this in the operating system:

```
int _rdrand64(uint64* val)
```
and
```
int _rdrand16(unsigned short* val)
```
There is also a real time clock available but it is unlikely to be particularly random in any CPU-bound process.

With this, I am looking at the best place to insert the code. Thinking `rand_unix.c` as a variant of `OPENSSL_RAND_SEED_OS` but not using `DEVRANDOM`.

The code already supports the RDRAND and RDSEED instructions on x86 look in `providers/implementations/rands/seeding`.

BTW, it ought to be possible to justify EGD as an entropy source as part of a FIPS validation.

> 
> 
> The code already supports the RDRAND and RDSEED instructions on x86 look in `providers/implementations/rands/seeding`.
> 
> BTW, it ought to be possible to justify EGD as an entropy source as part of a FIPS validation.

I'm really unsure how to plug those calls into the existing structure in `rand_cpu_x86.c`. The `_rdrand64` is not that standard in C or POSIX.

review_comments: I'd prefer to see an approach where `get_hardware_random_value` always exists and calls the appropriate code on a per platform basis (i.e. `OPENSSL_ia32_rdseed_bytes`, `OPENSSL_ia32_rdrand_bytes` or `_rdrand64`.  This isolates the conditional code to one place and gives us a generic function that can be used elsewhere if required.  It also gives us cross architecture possibilities.

That is actually a tiny bit closer to the original pull request, although I had everything in one procedure. I would be happy to further refactor this but I don't have a good basis of what platforms support the one of `OPENSSL_ia32_rdseed_bytes`, `OPENSSL_ia32_rdrand_bytes`. I can fold the discriminant into a commonly named procedure similar to the `get_hardware_random_value` for other platforms (better name?).

They are generated by `gen_random` in crypto/x86cpuid.pl and c`rypto/x86_64cpuid.pl`.  They should exist for all x86 and x86_64 platforms.

It is weird that your platform isn't detecting them, I though the CPUID feature for x86/x86_64 was universal by the time these were introduced.

I am surprised also, but the platform is not a traditional x86_64. It is Big Endian and has a whole bunch of strangeness. I have a related issue on the Itanium variant that I am working on for this also.
Coding style put a blank line between declarations and code.  Here and elsewhere.
I can't find any manual about _rdrand64, but does it take an unsigned long long, or an uint64_t?

> 
> 
> I can't find any manual about _rdrand64, but does it take an unsigned long long, or an uint64_t?

The method is a builtin intrinsic function on the HPE NonStop TNS/X platform. It is documented in their operating system API documentation site only, which is not SEO optimized. It takes a `uint64_t *` (which the compiler is not defining for some reason, but that is equivalent to `unsigned long long *` on the platform).
We use uint64_t in various files, so it really should be available.
Pushed a new change using uint64_t. Probably operator error last time.
